questions: How do you usually get around the place where you live?
Is there a way of travelling you avoid whenever you can? Why is that?
What's the traffic like where you live at busy times of day?
Has getting around your city become easier or harder over the last few years?
Do you think you'll still be travelling the same way five years from now?
Do you see yourself as more of a city person or a countryside person?
How often do you get out of the city into somewhere quieter?
What do you think people who live in the countryside enjoy that city people miss?
When you were a child, did you spend more time in cities or in the countryside?
Do you think more people your age will move out of big cities in the future?

part2.title: Describe a journey that did not go as planned.
bullets: where you were going and why
how you had planned to travel
what went wrong along the way
what you did when things went wrong
part2.explain: and explain how you felt during this journey, and whether you would do anything differently if it happened again.
followups: Did you eventually get where you were going?
Do you laugh about it now, or does it still annoy you?
Has that journey changed how you prepare for trips?

part3.q: How much do you think a long daily commute affects a person's quality of life?
followups: Which matters more — the length of the commute or how comfortable it is?
Do people get used to it over time, or does it wear them down?

part3.q: Why do people in some cities rely so heavily on cars, even for very short trips?
followups: Is that mainly about habit, or about how the city is built?
What would it take to change that behaviour?

part3.q: Do you think owning a car still carries the social status it once did?
followups: Has that changed within your lifetime?
Might it differ between smaller towns and big cities?

part3.q: Some people argue that public transport should be cheap even if taxpayers who never use it have to fund it. What's your view?
followups: Who benefits when a city has good public transport, apart from the passengers themselves?
Is there a limit to how far fares should be subsidised?

part3.q: Why do buses and trains in many countries struggle to attract people who can afford to drive?
followups: Is it a question of comfort, reliability, or image?
Can you think of anywhere that has managed to solve this?

part3.q: Some cities are removing road space from cars to make room for walking and cycling. Is that a good use of public space?
followups: What objections would drivers raise, and are they fair?
Would this work equally well in very hot or very cold climates?

part3.q: Should city governments actively discourage driving, or simply make the alternatives better and let people choose?
followups: Which approach do you think actually changes behaviour faster?
Is it fair to charge people for driving into a city centre?

part3.q: How does the way a city moves — its traffic, its transport — shape the character of the people who live there?
followups: Can you give an example of a city where you can see that connection?
Does a stressful transport system make a society less patient in general?

part3.q: Working from home was supposed to empty the roads, yet many cities are as congested as ever. Why might that be?
followups: Where do you think all that traffic is coming from, if fewer people commute?
Does this tell us anything about how hard travel behaviour is to predict?

part3.q: Looking twenty years ahead, how do you think people will move around cities differently from today?
followups: Which of those changes would benefit ordinary people most?
Is there a risk that new transport technology mainly serves the wealthy?

fc: Tells the Part 2 journey as a story with a spine — plan, disruption, decision, outcome — rather than a list of complaints, and keeps going without the examiner rescuing it.
Handles the change of direction naturally: "so at that point I had two options…" moves the story forward instead of stalling at the problem.
In Part 3, develops a position on fares or car dependence across three or four sentences before pausing — the follow-up prompts should rarely be needed.
Buys thinking time in English ("that's a tricky one, because it cuts both ways…") instead of long silences before the abstract policy questions.
Links ideas with cause-and-effect connectors that fit transport talk — "which is exactly why", "as a result", "the knock-on effect is" — without sounding mechanical.
lr: Precise transport vocabulary used naturally: congestion, rush hour, connection, detour, delay, commuter, fare, route — not textbook terms like 'conveyance'.
Collocations that native speakers actually use: "miss a connection", "stuck in traffic", "the last train home", "door-to-door journey", "peak fares".
Part 3 register shifts to policy language without strain: subsidise, invest in infrastructure, car-dependent, pedestrianise, congestion charge.
One or two natural idioms placed well — "we were cutting it fine", "back to square one" — beat a string of forced ones.
Paraphrases smoothly when a word escapes: "one of those electric scooters you rent by the minute" is a Band 8 recovery, not a failure.
gra: Past narrative tenses carry the Part 2 story: "we were halfway there when the engine gave out", "the bus had already left by the time we arrived".
Third conditional and mixed conditionals appear where the cue card invites them: "If I'd checked the platform, we would have made it."
Comparatives and measured quantifiers structure Part 3 answers: "far more reliable than", "a fraction of the cost", "nowhere near enough capacity".
Concessive framing on the policy questions: "Even if fares were free, plenty of people would still drive, because…".
Passives fit naturally when talking about cities being changed: "whole streets have been pedestrianised", "the line was extended in 2023".
pron: The Part 2 story has audible drama — pace quickens slightly at the crisis, slows for the reflection — without becoming a performance.
Stress lands on the contrast words the topic invites: "it should have taken two hours — it took SEVEN."
Numbers, times and platform-style details are crisp and unambiguous; "thirteen" and "thirty" never blur.
Multi-syllable topic words are stressed correctly: conGEStion, inFRAstructure, pedeSTRIan, reliaBIlity.
Chunking supports the longer Part 3 sentences — a brief pause after "the real problem is…" lets the point land.

band9.part1: Answer directly, then add one specific detail or reason — two to four sentences, no speeches. For "Is there a way of travelling you avoid whenever you can?" a Band 9 answer commits to something real: "Auto-rickshaws at rush hour — you spend twenty minutes haggling and then sit breathing exhaust fumes in a queue, so unless it's raining I'd honestly rather walk." The specificity — the haggling, the fumes, the exception for rain — is what separates it from "I don't like traffic, it is very crowded."
part2: Set-up — one or two sentences establishing the stakes: where you were headed, why it mattered that day, and what the plan was supposed to look like.
The plan in motion — briefly show the journey starting normally, so the disruption lands with contrast: "everything was on schedule until…".
The moment it went wrong — pin down the exact point of failure with concrete detail: the cancelled departure on the board, the road closed for a procession, the flat tyre an hour from anywhere.
Your response — the decisions you made under pressure, including the option you rejected; this is where the story shows judgement, not just bad luck.
How you felt — trace the arc honestly: irritation, then something else — resignation, unexpected calm, even enjoyment once you surrendered to it.
Looking back — close by answering the cue card's final question head-on: what you'd do differently, or why you've decided some journeys are simply beyond planning.

part3.method: Answer → Explain → Example → Alternative View → Evaluation
part3.question: Some people argue that public transport should be cheap even if taxpayers who never use it have to fund it. What's your view?
framework: Answer: commit to a position — e.g. yes, cheap fares are a fair use of general taxation, because everyone benefits whether they ride or not.
Explain: give the mechanism — every full bus takes dozens of cars off the road, so even lifelong drivers gain through lighter traffic, cleaner air and workers who can actually reach their jobs.

Example: anchor it in something concrete — cities that slashed fares, or a flat-rate monthly ticket like Germany's, saw ridership jump; compare that with cities where fares crept up and buses emptied out.

Alternative view: concede genuinely — subsidies can be regressive if they prop up half-empty routes, and there's a reasonable argument that the money would do more good in service frequency than in ticket prices.

Evaluate: land the judgement — cheap fares are necessary but not sufficient; the deeper point is that transport is infrastructure like street lighting, and nobody asks street lighting to turn a profit.

mistakes.title: Narrating the itinerary instead of the disruption
mistakes.detail: The cue card is about a journey that went wrong. Candidates spend ninety seconds on the destination, the hotel and the sightseeing, and mention the twelve-hour delay in one sentence. The disruption — and your response to it — is the story.

mistakes.title: A journey with no plan to go wrong
mistakes.detail: "We went to Manali and it was very nice" fails the card at the root. If nothing deviated from a plan, the examiner can't credit the 'what went wrong' or 'what you did' bullets. Pick a trip with a genuine derailment, however small.

mistakes.title: Blaming without deciding
mistakes.detail: Ten sentences about how terrible the airline was, and none about what you actually did next. The strongest tellings centre your decisions — rebook, wait, split up, give up — because decisions generate the language of judgement the examiner rewards.

mistakes.title: One-word Part 1 answers about your own city
mistakes.detail: "How do you get around?" — "By bus." You travel these streets every day; two sentences with a reason ("mostly by metro, because the last stretch to my office is a ten-minute walk and it beats sitting in traffic") is the natural register.

mistakes.title: Reciting a memorised 'pollution' essay in Part 3
mistakes.detail: The questions here are about commuting, fares, street space and behaviour — not a general environment speech. A prepared paragraph about factories and global warming is visibly off-target and costs coherence marks.

mistakes.title: Treating 'should governments discourage driving?' as having one safe answer
mistakes.detail: There is no examiner-approved position. "Yes, ban cars" argued thinly scores below "honestly, I think punishing drivers backfires — here's why" argued well. The marks are in the reasoning, not the stance.

mistakes.title: Vagueness where the topic begs for numbers
mistakes.detail: Transport talk lives on specifics: a forty-minute commute, fares that doubled in five years, a bus every four minutes. "Very far", "very expensive" and "many problems" flatten every answer into Band 6 territory.

mistakes.title: Confusing 'travel', 'trip' and 'journey'
mistakes.detail: "A travel" is a classic error on this exact topic. Travel is usually uncountable; you take a trip or describe a journey. Getting the topic's core nouns wrong in Part 2 is an avoidable dent in Lexical Resource.

mistakes.title: Present tense creeping into a past story
mistakes.detail: Under pressure, candidates slide into "so we are waiting and the bus is not coming". The narrative tenses — was waiting, had already left, would have made it — are precisely what this cue card exists to sample.

mistakes.title: Predicting flying cars in the twenty-years question
mistakes.detail: The future-of-mobility question rewards grounded reasoning — driverless fleets changing car ownership, e-bikes eating short trips, cities pricing road space — not science fiction. One plausible change explained beats five fantasies listed.
